title: Round willow bread basket
subtitle: A traditional round-base basket for bread, fruit, and produce
excerpt: A round willow basket with a flat base, 30 cm across, 12 cm deep, with a double-wale border. Brown willow for the stakes, buff for the weavers. A classic first basket: the round base is more forgiving than an oval and the form is used in every British basket-weaving tradition.
sourceNotes: Dorothy Wright, The Complete Guide to Basket Weaving (1977), public domain in territories under life+50 rules; traditional British brown-and-buff round-base pattern.

glossaryTerms.definition: The upright structural rods of a basket that form the frame for the woven sides. Stakes are heavier-gauge rods than weavers.
The thinner rods woven between the stakes to build up the sides of the basket.
A pointed steel spike used to open up the weave to insert new rods or to thread the border work.
A long diagonal cut at the base of a rod to give a pointed insertion tip. Cut with secateurs in one stroke.

content.text: A round bread basket is the classic starting project in British willow weaving. The round base is made from a slath of eight sticks woven through with four working
weaver
s (pairing weave), upset with a four-rod wale, and sided with a plain weave to 12 cm depth. The border is a three-rod behind-one. At 30 cm across, it holds a standard-sized loaf or a punnet of fruit.
Willow is worked wet. The rods must be soaked in a trough until fully flexible (4 to 12 hours depending on size) and then kept damp throughout the session by covering with a damp cloth.
Materials
Base sticks: 8 rods of brown willow, 35 cm long, approximately 8 mm diameter at the butt.
Stake

s: 16 rods of brown willow, 70 cm long, 6 to 7 mm at the butt. Weavers: 60 to 80 buff willow rods, 90 cm to 1.2 m, 3 to 4 mm at the butt. Wale rods: 12 brown willow rods, 70 cm, 5 to 6 mm at the butt.
Soaking

Soak all rods in a soaking trough for 4 hours (buff) to 8 hours (brown). Buff willow is already treated (steamed) and soaks faster. Brown willow (unpeeled dried rod) needs longer. After soaking, wrap in a damp cloth and leave for one hour to mellow before use.
Method
Step 1: Make the slath
Group the 8 base sticks into two groups of four. Pierce the centre of one group with the
bodkin
and thread the other group of four through the gap. The cross of sticks is called the slath. It should sit flat and even, with four sticks in each direction.
Step 2: Tie in and pair the slath

Insert two buff weavers into the slath alongside the pierced sticks. Use pairing weave to go around the cross of sticks, treating each group of four as one unit for the first two rounds. After two rounds, open the groups: each stick now becomes a single stake and the pairing weave separates them, going in and out of each individual stick. Continue pairing for six rounds.
Step 3: Insert the side stakes
Cut a
slype

on each of the 16 side stakes. Insert one stake beside each base stick (one on each side) using the bodkin to open a channel. Push the stakes down 8 to 10 cm alongside the base sticks. Trim the base sticks to 1 cm beyond the outer edge of the base weave.
Step 4: Upset with a four-rod wale

Turn the base over and prop on the basket weights, or hold on your knee. Fold the 16 stakes upward at 90 degrees. Insert four wale rods and weave a four-rod behind-one wale for three rounds. The wale locks the base weave and sets the angle of the stakes. Use the rapping iron to press the wale down tightly after each round.
Step 5: Side with pairing weave

Insert buff weavers in pairs and side the basket with pairing weave to 10 cm height. Join in new weavers at the butt end (place the new butt alongside the old one for 4 stakes before pulling out the old one). Keep the stakes vertical and evenly spaced; use your hands to set the flare angle as you work.
Step 6: Final wale and border

Weave a final three-round four-rod wale to set the rim height. Work the border: take each stake in turn, kink it at the rim, thread it behind one stake, in front of two, behind one, and cut off inside the basket. The three-behind-one border is the standard beginner border and produces a neat, rounded rim.
Finishing

No oil or coating is applied to a willow basket. The raw surface is the finished surface. Trim any loose ends with secateurs after the basket has dried for 24 hours. Allow to dry fully (three to five days) before use.

attrs.symptom: The base is dishing (curving upward at the rim)
attrs.cause: The pairing weave tension was uneven, pulling the base into a bowl shape.
attrs.fix: Weight the base with a board and a heavy object while working. Keep tension consistent around the base and check flatness after every two rounds.

attrs.symptom: Stakes are splitting when folded up
attrs.cause: The rods were not fully mellowed after soaking, or the stakes are too large in diameter.
attrs.fix: Use stakes that are 6 to 7 mm at the butt for a 30 cm basket. If splitting begins, sponge warm water onto the split area and allow to absorb for five minutes before continuing.
